title: update_user (PATCH) can remove the last admin, bypassing the last-admin guard that delete_user enforces and causing permanent admin lockout
detail: delete_user (lines 109-118) refuses to remove the last remaining admin, but update_user has no equivalent guard. An admin can set role=UserRole.user (line 63-65) or is_active=False (line 60-62) on the only admin account (or on themselves). Both paths bump token_version, invalidating the affected session immediately. Once the sole admin is demoted or deactivated, require_admin (api/auth/deps.py) rejects everyone: no user can reach any /api/v1/admin endpoint to undo it. The 'at least one admin' invariant is enforced inconsistently across the two mutation paths.
failure_scenario: Deployment with a single admin. Admin issues PATCH /api/v1/admin/users/{own_id} with {"role":"user"} (or {"is_active":false}). Server accepts it, sets role/is_active, bumps token_version. Next request 401s; there are now 0 active admins. Every admin endpoint returns 403/401 forever, requiring manual DB edit or scripts/create_admin.py to recover.
suggested_fix: Before committing a role downgrade or deactivation in update_user, if the target is currently an admin and the change would drop the active-admin count to 0, count remaining active admins (role==admin AND is_active) excluding this change and raise HTTP 409 (reuse the same guard used in delete_user). Also forbid an admin from demoting/deactivating their own account.
verify_reasoning: Traced api/routers/admin.py directly. delete_user (lines 109-118) explicitly counts admins (select func.count where role==admin) and raises 409 if admin_count <= 1. update_user (lines 55-72) has NO such guard: req.role sets user.role unconditionally (63-65) and req.is_active sets user.is_active unconditionally (60-62), each bumping token_version (62/65) which invalidates the affected session on next request. Both handlers are gated only by require_admin; there is no service-layer or model-level invariant enforcing "at least one admin" — the mutation is inline in the handler. An admin PATCHing the sole admin account (own or other) with {"role":"user"} or {"is_active":false} succeeds, commits, and leaves 0 active admins; require_admin then rejects everyone, requiring manual DB edit / create_admin.py to recover. The invariant is enforced inconsistently across the two mutation paths exactly as claimed. High severity is warranted: permanent privileged-access lockout / self-inflicted DoS on the admin surface, reachable by any admin including via self-demotion.

title: SHAP endpoint reports success=True even when the model wrapper silently fails and returns all-zero attributions
detail: In shap_analysis the model_wrapper wraps model.predict in a blanket `except Exception: return np.zeros((1, output_chunk))`. compute_shap_importance's perturbation fallback computes importance as (baseline_pred - perturbed_pred); if every predict call throws (e.g. the Darts model requires future/static covariates, a specific series length, or past_covariates that were not reconstructed), all wrapper calls return identical zeros, so every feature_importance / event_importance / shap_value becomes 0.0. The endpoint (lines 282-288) then unconditionally sets success=True, so the caller receives a scientifically meaningless 'all features contribute 0' result presented as a successful explanation.
failure_scenario: A TFT/transformer model whose predict() needs future_covariates (not supplied by model_wrapper) -> every predict raises -> wrapper returns zeros -> perturbation SHAP yields feature_importance={col:0.0,...} -> POST /shap returns 200 {success:true, feature_importance all zeros}, misleading the analyst into thinking no feature matters.
suggested_fix: Have model_wrapper record/propagate failures (e.g. count exceptions) and make compute_shap_importance / shap_analysis return success=False with an error_message when the wrapper never produced a valid (non-fallback) prediction, instead of silently substituting zeros.
verify_reasoning: Traced api/routers/explainability.py:250-288 and dashboard/utils/explainability/feature_importance.py:201-364. The model_wrapper (lines 257-268) catches all exceptions from model.predict() and returns np.zeros((1, output_chunk)); it only supplies series and (conditionally) past_covariates, never future_covariates. In _compute_perturbation_shap, baseline_pred and every perturbed_pred come solely from model_wrapper, and importances are computed as baseline_pred - perturbed_pred (lines 324/335/344/356). If every predict call raises, all outputs are 0, so feature_importance, event_importance, and shap_values are all uniformly 0.0. The TimeSHAP path (tried first) also produces all-zero Shapley values when f returns constant zeros. Crucially the /shap endpoint hardcodes success=True (line 284) with no all-zero or failure check, and the perturbation result carries no 'success' key — contrast the attention endpoint at line 196 which propagates result.get('success', False). Concrete failure: a TFT/transformer model that requires future_covariates (never passed by the wrapper) makes every predict throw, so the analyst receives HTTP 200 {success:true, feature_importance: all 0.0}, a scientifically meaningless result masquerading as a valid explanation. Defect is real and the exact scenario holds. Severity high given the project's emphasis on scientific correctness and the silent, undetectable nature of the failure; it is a diagnostic/explainability endpoint rather than core data, but presenting garbage as a successful standardized explanation is a genuine integrity issue. Suggested fix: have model_wrapper record/raise on repeated failures (or a failure counter), have _compute_perturbation_shap flag when baseline/all perturbations collapse to a constant, and set success based on result state (e.g. detect all-zero importances or propagate a 'success'/'error' key) instead of hardcoding True.

title: Cancelling a running training does not stop the GPU work and lets a second job start concurrently on the single shared GPU
detail: The training thread only checks `task.stop_event.is_set()` once, at line 138, BEFORE calling `run_training_pipeline`. The pipeline call (lines 166-192) is passed no `task`, `stop_event`, or cancellation callback, so once the (long, epoch-heavy) training loop starts it cannot be interrupted. Meanwhile `task_manager.cancel()` (task_manager.py:76-81) immediately sets status=CANCELLED. The `start_training` guard (lines 252-255) only treats PENDING/RUNNING tasks as 'active'. So after a cancel the still-running thread is no longer counted as active, and a NEW training request passes the 409 guard and starts a second training. The MEMORY invariant is 'Single shared GPU: only one training at a time' — this breaks it.
failure_scenario: User A starts a 200-epoch NHiTS training. At epoch 5 they hit /training/{id}/cancel. UI shows CANCELLED but the thread keeps training the full 200 epochs on the RTX A6000. User B (or A) now calls /training/start; the active-task filter finds nothing PENDING/RUNNING, so a second training launches → two concurrent trainings contend for the 48 GB GPU → CUDA OOM / crashed runs.
suggested_fix: Pass `task.stop_event` (or the task) into `run_training_pipeline` and have the training loop poll it between epochs (e.g. via a Lightning callback that raises/stops when set); and/or include CANCELLED-but-thread-alive tasks in the active-guard (check `task.thread.is_alive()`), so a new job cannot start while the GPU is still busy.
verify_reasoning: Traced the full path. (1) No cancellation propagation into training: in api/routers/training.py the only stop check is `task.stop_event.is_set()` at line 138, executed BEFORE `run_training_pipeline` is called (lines 166-192). The pipeline signature (dashboard/utils/training.py:472-501) has no `task`, `stop_event`, or cancellation-callback parameter, and grep for `stop_event|should_stop|Interrupt|task_manager|.cancel(` inside training.py returns nothing — so once PyTorch Lightning `fit()` begins (200 epochs on the RTX A6000) it cannot be interrupted. Python threads cannot be force-killed, and the thread is `daemon=True`, so it keeps running to completion. (2) Cancel flips status early: `task_manager.cancel()` (task_manager.py:76-81) sets `status=CANCELLED` immediately while the thread is still running. (3) The concurrency guard in `start_training` (training.py:252-255) only counts tasks with status in (PENDING, RUNNING) as active. After cancel, the still-running task is CANCELLED, so it is no longer active; a new /start request passes the 409 guard (lines 256-267) and launches a second `_run_training_thread`. Two trainings then contend for the single shared GPU — exactly the invariant the code comment at line 258 asserts ("Single shared GPU: only one training at a time"), leading to CUDA OOM/crashed runs. Both halves of the failure scenario hold. Suggested fix: pass the task's stop_event into run_training_pipeline and wire a Lightning callback (e.g. on_train_batch_end/on_train_epoch_end) that raises to abort fit when set; and/or count CANCELLED-but-thread-alive tasks (task.thread.is_alive()) as active in the start guard, or join/await thread termination before allowing a new job.

title: CounterfactualPage builds window GT with full-length dates but null-filtered values, misaligning every value after a gap
detail: currentWindowData returns `dates` as the raw slice (length N) but `values` as `values.filter(v !== null)` (length M ≤ N). Downstream consumers zip them by index: computeMonthlyIps(dates, values) pairs dates[i] with values[i] (lib/ips.ts:109-116), and CFComparisonView plots x=gtDates, y=gtValues by index (lines 362-364 here → CFComparisonView.tsx:112-121). As soon as one null exists before the end of the window, every subsequent value is shifted onto the wrong date. Piezometric daily test series routinely contain gaps, and the CF prediction window (output_chunk_length) can span a month boundary, so a value gets attributed to the wrong calendar month, producing wrong monthly z-scores, wrong IPS classes, and ultimately a wrong quality-gate verdict (qualified/partial/not_qualified). The same misalignment also corrupts predIps via windowPredValues (lines 154-185).
failure_scenario: Model window = dates [2024-01-30, 2024-01-31(null), 2024-02-01, 2024-02-02], test_values = [10.0, null, 8.0, 8.1]. After filter, values = [10.0, 8.0, 8.1]. computeMonthlyIps pairs 2024-01-31→8.0 and 2024-02-01→8.1, so February's mean is computed from January's reading (and vice-versa). The IPS class for Feb is wrong, the quality-gate banner may flip from 'qualified' to 'not_qualified', and the observed (green) line on the CF comparison chart is drawn one day early for every point after the gap.
suggested_fix: Keep dates and values in lockstep: filter as pairs, e.g. build an array of {date, value} from the slice, drop entries whose value is null, then split back into aligned dates[] and values[]. Return the filtered dates alongside the filtered values so all consumers (computeMonthlyIps, CFComparisonView, windowPredValues) use matching indices.
verify_reasoning:
Traced the full chain in the real code. CounterfactualPage.tsx:149-151 builds `currentWindowData` with `dates = test_values.slice(...)` (full length N, keeps every timestamp including gap days) but `values = ...slice(...).filter(v !== null)` (compacted length M ≤ N). The `.filter(v !== null)` proves test_values is `(number|null)[]` and that nulls are expected — piezometric daily series routinely have gaps.

Downstream consumers pair the two arrays strictly by index:
- computeMonthlyIps (lib/ips.ts:109-116) loops `for i in dates.length` and does `groups.get(yearMonth).vals.push(values[i])`, pairing dates[i] with values[i]. Its internal `!isNaN(values[i]) && values[i]!==null` guard does NOT rehabilitate alignment — the nulls were already removed upstream, so index i on/after the first gap reads the wrong element (and trailing i≥M read undefined, harmlessly skipped). Reproduced the claimed scenario: dates=[01-30,01-31,02-01,02-02], values(filtered)=[10.0,8.0,8.1] → Jan group gets {10.0,8.0}, Feb group gets {8.1}, whereas correct is Jan{10.0}, Feb{8.0,8.1}. Monthly means, z-scores, and IPS classes are wrong.
- gtIps (line 179) and predIps (line 184) both feed computeQualityGate (line 189), so a flipped monthly IPS class can change the qualified/partial/not_qualified verdict (line 192).
- CFComparisonView receives gtDates=full dates, gtValues=filtered values (CounterfactualPage.tsx:362-363) and Plotly zips x=gtDates, y=gtValues by index (CFComparisonView.tsx:112-121), so the observed (green) line is drawn shifted for every point after a gap.

The only condition is at least one null appearing before the window's last element and the window (output_chunk_length) spanning a month boundary — both are normal for the data, and the filter's presence shows nulls occur. Fix: filter dates and values together (e.g. build pairs, drop where value is null, then unzip) so both arrays stay index-aligned; do the same for windowPredValues/predIps.

Severity high is appropriate: the defect silently corrupts the scientific IPS classification and the model qualification verdict, which is the entire purpose of the page. Not critical only because it is an internal model-exploration/qualification tool rather than a public data output.

title: SPI/precip observed window uses raw SUM over rounded coords, double-counting float-doublon cells, while the gamma/climatology reference weighted-averages the same variants
detail: The observed-window queries for SPI (line 732: `SUM(total_precipitation) AS window_sum ... GROUP BY round(latitude::numeric,1), round(longitude::numeric,1)`) and for the precipitation branch of /anomaly (line 868) SUM every raw row that rounds into a 0.1 cell. For the known ERA5 float-doublon cells (same physical cell present under two slightly different float coordinates from backfill vs incremental loads), any month that has rows under BOTH coordinate variants is summed twice. This is exactly the double-count the reference path deliberately avoids: `_era5_spi_reference`/`_scan_monthly_cell_stats` compute a per-variant monthly SUM and then merge variants with a count-weighted AVERAGE (lines 513-524, 582-591, comment 'same physical cell duplicated by float rounding — average, don't double-count'), and `_era5_precip_climatology` does the same (lines 292-302). So the gamma / climatology baseline is fitted at the 1x accumulation scale but the observed window can be ~2x for doublon cells that overlap in the observed month (the backfill/incremental seam). The two paths are methodologically inconsistent for the very cells the doublon guard exists for.
failure_scenario: A physical cell whose latest complete month is present under both float-coordinate variants (backfill+incremental seam) yields window_sum ~= 2x the true accumulation. The gamma CDF for ~2x the fitted scale returns ~1.0, clamped to 0.999 -> SPI pinned to +3.09 -> classified EXTREMEMENT_HAUT (extreme-wet) on the map even during a normal or dry month; /anomaly precipitation shows a spurious ~+100% anomaly for the same cells.
suggested_fix: Make the observed window canonicalize doublons the same way the reference does: aggregate per (raw lat, raw lon, month) SUM first, then merge the rounded-0.1 variants with a count-weighted average (as in _scan_monthly_cell_stats) before accumulating the N-month window — do not SUM raw rows across variants. Apply the identical fix to the /anomaly precipitation query at line 868.
verify_reasoning:
Traced both paths in api/routers/observatory_era5.py and api/era5_anomaly.py.

REFERENCE path (doublon-guarded): _era5_spi_reference (lines 490-524) and _era5_precip_climatology (lines 268-303) both group by RAW (lat,lon,year,month) to get a per-variant monthly SUM, then round to 0.1° and merge float-doublon variants with a COUNT-weighted AVERAGE (sw/sn), with the explicit comment "same physical cell duplicated by float rounding — average, don't double-count." So the fitted gamma / climatology normal is at the 1x monthly-accumulation scale. _scan_monthly_cell_stats (582-591) does the same for the warmers.

OBSERVED path (NOT guarded): line 732 (`SUM(total_precipitation) ... GROUP BY round(latitude::numeric,1), round(longitude::numeric,1)`) and the /anomaly precip branch at line 868 sum EVERY raw row falling into a 0.1° cell. For a doublon cell whose observed month(s) carry rows under both float-coordinate variants, both variants' monthly totals are added → ~2x for those months. n_months uses COUNT(DISTINCT date_trunc('month',...)) so it stays == window (unaffected by duplication) and the cell is NOT filtered by compute_spi_grid's n_months<window guard (era5_anomaly.py:116) or compute_precip_anomalies' guard (line 175). The inflated sum flows through: gamma.cdf(~2x, fitted at 1x scale) → ~1.0, clamped to 0.999 (line 130) → z = norm.ppf(0.999) = +3.09 → classified extreme-wet; precip anomaly = (2x - 1x)/1x = ~+100%. Arithmetic holds exactly as claimed.

Corroborating evidence the SUM path is the outlier: the STI/temp observed path (lines 793-809) uses AVG within-month then AVG across months, which is inherently immune to duplicate-variant rows — so the precip SUM branch is uniquely unprotected while its own reference is protected. The methodological asymmetry is unambiguous in code.

The one runtime-dependent element is whether doublon cells actually carry both variants inside a selected observed window. Project memory (era5-coordinate-precision-bug: ~1300 grilles doublons backfill vs incrémental) documents that doublons exist in gold.era5_grid, and the reference path merges variants at EVERY (year,month) — implying variants coexist across many months, not just an isolated seam. The /spi and /anomaly endpoints accept an arbitrary date param, so windows straddling the backfill/incremental overlap are reachable by the user, not just the latest month. Defect is real and the failure mechanism is verified; keeping severity medium since concrete impact is limited to the subset of doublon cells whose selected window contains overlapping variant rows.

Suggested fix: mirror the reference — nest a per-(rounded-cell, month) aggregation that weighted-averages the variants' monthly sum, then SUM across the N months (as _spi_ref_from_cells does), instead of a flat SUM over rounded coords.

title: Hydro get_station LATERAL reference subquery omits the lower QmnJ sentinel bound, so negative Hub'Eau sentinels pollute the reference median and drop the current value
detail: Every other flow-reading path filters BOTH sentinel bounds: get_percentiles uses `resultat_obs_elab > _QMNJ_MIN_VALID AND < _QMNJ_MAX_VALID` (lines 184-185) and get_ssfi uses `resultat_moyen > 0 AND resultat_moyen < :max_v` (line 380). But the LATERAL `lm` subquery in get_station guards only the UPPER bound: line 595 `m2.resultat_moyen IS NOT NULL AND m2.resultat_moyen < 1e8` (for the per-calendar-month percentile_cont(0.5) `month_median`) and line 600 `m.resultat_moyen IS NOT NULL AND m.resultat_moyen < 1e8` (for the latest-month `ref_value` picked via ORDER BY mois DESC). Hub'Eau QmnJ sentinels for missing data include large NEGATIVE values (e.g. -4e6, -1.5e5, which are < -1e4 = _QMNJ_MIN_VALID) that are < 1e8 and thus pass this filter. Two consequences: (a) the percentile_cont(0.5) median is computed over a set containing negative sentinels, dragging `index_month_median` below the true monthly median; (b) if the latest month's aggregate is itself a negative sentinel it is selected as `ref_value`, then `_qmnj_to_m3_s(-4e6)` returns None (line 612-615), so `index_ref_value` becomes null even though valid earlier months exist. These fields are returned to the frontend as the reference/current-value context for the station index.
failure_scenario: A hydro station whose fct_monthly_hydro has a January aggregate of resultat_moyen = -400000 (sentinel-derived) and whose most recent month is also a sentinel: GET /api/v1/observatory/hydro/stations/{code}. index_month_median for January is computed including -400000 (median pulled far too low, and after /1000 conversion may itself become None), and index_ref_value comes back null despite the station having valid recent flow — the detail panel shows a wrong or missing reference line while the SSFI classification (from the materialized fixed-reference tables) looks normal, an internal inconsistency.
suggested_fix: Add the lower sentinel bound to both the inner and outer LATERAL filters to match get_ssfi/get_percentiles, e.g. `AND m2.resultat_moyen > 0 AND m2.resultat_moyen < 1e8` on line 595 and `AND m.resultat_moyen > 0 AND m.resultat_moyen < 1e8` on line 600 (or use `> _QMNJ_MIN_VALID` if legitimately-small non-positive flows must be kept). Use the shared _QMNJ_MIN_VALID/_QMNJ_MAX_VALID constants rather than the hardcoded 1e8 for consistency.
verify_reasoning: Verified in api/routers/observatory_hydro.py. Constants (43-44): _QMNJ_MAX_VALID=1e8, _QMNJ_MIN_VALID=-1e4. The get_station LATERAL subquery filters ONLY the upper bound: line 595 (`m2.resultat_moyen IS NOT NULL AND m2.resultat_moyen < 1e8` for the per-month percentile_cont(0.5) month_median) and line 600 (same for the ORDER BY mois DESC LIMIT 1 ref_value). By contrast, every sibling flow-reading path guards BOTH sentinel bounds: get_percentiles (184-185) uses `resultat_obs_elab > :min_valid AND < :max_valid`, and get_ssfi (380) uses `resultat_moyen > 0 AND resultat_moyen < :max_v` — on the SAME gold.fct_monthly_hydro.resultat_moyen column, with the explicit comment 'positive only; sentinels already filtered'. This is strong evidence negative sentinels (e.g. -4e6, -400000, called out in the code comment at 173-174) do appear in that column, and the get_station LATERAL is the odd one out. _qmnj_to_m3_s (61-68) maps any v <= -1e4 to None. Consequences trace cleanly: (a) percentile_cont(0.5) median includes negative sentinels that pass `< 1e8`, dragging index_month_median below the true monthly median (and if the resulting median is itself <= -1e4 it is converted to None); (b) if the most-recent month's aggregate is a negative sentinel it survives the `< 1e8` filter, is chosen by ORDER BY mois DESC LIMIT 1 as ref_value, then _qmnj_to_m3_s returns None so index_ref_value is null despite valid earlier months. Both fields are returned via the HydroStation response (585-586, converted at 612-615), producing a wrong/missing reference line while the SSFI class (from the fixed-reference materialized tables) stays normal — the claimed internal inconsistency. Fix: add `AND m.resultat_moyen > :min_valid` / `AND m2.resultat_moyen > :min_valid` and bind _QMNJ_MIN_VALID. Severity medium: data-coherence defect on a secondary reference/display field, not a crash or leak; depends on the underlying data actually containing negative monthly sentinels, which the sibling guards and comments strongly imply.

title: WFS proxy caches and serves upstream error bodies because it only checks the HTTP status code, not the payload
detail: _fetch_wfs_raw treats any HTTP 200 as success (resp.status_code != 200). OGC/WFS servers such as the SANDRE geo endpoint routinely return an OWS ExceptionReport (or an HTML error page) with HTTP 200 rather than a 4xx/5xx. The router then gzips that error body, stores it in Redis under key `junon:obs_wfs_{layer_id}:{h}` with WFS_TTL=86400, and serves it to the client with media_type='application/json'. There is no validation that the body is actually GeoJSON (no check for a FeatureCollection / content-type). Combined with the 24h TTL this poisons the cache: a single transient upstream hiccup is served as a broken layer for a full day even after SANDRE recovers.
failure_scenario: Client requests GET /api/v1/observatory/wfs/secteur-hydro?bbox=... while SANDRE is briefly degraded and replies HTTP 200 with an <ows:ExceptionReport> XML body. status_code==200, so the code gzips and setex()s the XML for 24h and returns it as application/json. The frontend map's JSON.parse throws and the secteur-hydro overlay stays empty for 24h; every subsequent request with the same bbox hits the poisoned cache entry.
suggested_fix: After fetch, validate the Content-Type is JSON/GeoJSON and that json.loads(...) yields a dict with type=='FeatureCollection' (or at least a 'features' key) before caching; on validation failure raise HTTPException(502) and do NOT setex. Optionally cache errors with a short negative TTL instead of WFS_TTL.
verify_reasoning: Traced api/routers/observatory_wfs.py fully. _fetch_wfs_raw (line 79-83) validates ONLY resp.status_code != 200; on any 200 it returns resp.content with zero payload inspection (no Content-Type check, no FeatureCollection/GeoJSON sniff). In get_wfs_layer, line 117 calls _fetch_wfs_raw, line 118 gzips the bytes, and lines 120-122 unconditionally setex the compressed body under junon:obs_wfs_{layer_id}:{h} with WFS_TTL=86400 (24h), then lines 127-132 return it as media_type='application/json'. There is no branch that distinguishes a valid GeoJSON body from an error body before caching. This matches the claim exactly. The only external dependency is whether SANDRE/OGC returns an <ows:ExceptionReport> (or HTML) with HTTP 200 — which is standard, well-documented OWS/WFS behavior (OGC services routinely wrap ServiceExceptionReport/ExceptionReport in a 200 response), so the scenario is realistic, not speculative. Note that pure connection failures raise inside httpx.get and propagate as an uncaught exception (no caching), so those specifically don't poison the cache; but an HTTP-200 error body does get cached for 24h and breaks the frontend's JSON.parse, keeping the overlay empty for every subsequent same-bbox request until TTL expiry or manual eviction. Defect and failure scenario both hold. Severity medium is appropriate: reference/overlay data, not a security or data-integrity issue, but a 24h TTL amplifies a transient upstream hiccup into a day-long broken layer. Suggested fix: after the status check, verify Content-Type contains json (or parse and confirm top-level type=='FeatureCollection') before compressing/caching; on mismatch log resp.text[:200] and raise 502 without writing to Redis.

title: Brute-force lockout and rate limiting fail open when Redis is unavailable
detail: All three protections degrade to 'no protection' when Redis is down or errors: `is_locked` returns False if `get_redis()` is None or on any exception (lines 29-35), `register_failure` returns without recording failures (lines 40-49), and `enforce_ip_rate_limit` returns immediately if Redis is None and swallows exceptions (lines 63-80). Because these are the only brute-force controls (verified in the login flow of api/routers/auth.py), a Redis outage — which an attacker can also induce by flooding — completely removes account lockout AND per-IP rate limiting simultaneously.
failure_scenario: Redis becomes unreachable (crash, network partition, or memory pressure from attacker traffic). `enforce_ip_rate_limit` no-ops, `is_locked` always returns False, and failures are never counted. An attacker can then make unlimited high-rate password-guessing requests against /api/v1/auth/login with no lockout and no 429, enabling offline-speed online brute force.
suggested_fix: Fail closed for at least one control: when Redis is unavailable, either reject login with 503 or apply a conservative in-process fallback rate limit. At minimum, log at WARNING (not debug) and add health alerting; do not let a Redis error path silently disable all auth throttling.
verify_reasoning: Read api/auth/ratelimit.py, api/routers/auth.py, and api/cache.py. All three protections fail open exactly as described: is_locked (l.22-30) returns False when get_redis() is None or on any exception; register_failure (l.32-43) no-ops when Redis is None or on exception so failures are never persisted; enforce_ip_rate_limit (l.54-72) returns immediately when Redis is None and swallows all non-HTTP exceptions so no 429 is emitted. get_redis() (api/cache.py l.26-28) returns _client, which is None if the pool failed to build and never live-checked, so operations against a down Redis raise inside the try blocks and get swallowed. The login flow (auth.py l.44-60) relies solely on these three functions with no DB-backed fallback, so a Redis outage removes account lockout and per-IP rate limiting simultaneously. Defect is real. I downgraded severity from high to medium: passwords are verified with a real hash (verify_password), so it is online brute force at server hashing throughput, not the claimed offline-speed; and it requires a Redis-unavailable precondition. Still a legitimate fail-open of the only brute-force controls; fix is to fail closed (503 / in-process fallback limiter) and add a DB-backed failure counter.

title: delete_user performs irreversible artifact erasure before the DB transaction commits, risking data loss with the user row still present if commit fails
detail: erase_user_artifacts(uid) (line 120) irreversibly deletes filesystem dataset directories (shutil.rmtree) and MLflow runs (client.delete_run) BEFORE db.delete(user) and db.commit() (lines 121-127). If the commit later fails (DB error, connection drop, or a concurrently-running request), the user's artifacts are already gone but the user account and its auth history remain, leaving an inconsistent half-deleted state that cannot be rolled back. The erasure is not part of the transaction and is not retried.
failure_scenario: Admin deletes user X. erase_user_artifacts wipes X's prepared-dataset directories and MLflow runs. db.commit() then fails (e.g., DB connection reset). The API returns 500, X still exists as an active account, but all their models/datasets are permanently destroyed and no admin_user_deleted event is persisted (record_event was added to the same rolled-back transaction).
suggested_fix: Reorder so the DB delete + audit event commit first, then invoke erase_user_artifacts (best-effort) after a successful commit; or move erasure into a post-commit background task keyed by the (already-deleted) user_id. Ensure the deletion audit event is recorded durably regardless of erasure outcome.

title: Training thread unconditionally overwrites CANCELLED status with COMPLETED when the pipeline finishes

Because cancellation cannot actually stop the pipeline (see prior finding), a cancelled job runs to completion and then flips its own status from CANCELLED back to COMPLETED, and the trained model is registered in MLflow as if nothing was cancelled.

The pipeline nonetheless completes minutes later, line 194 resets status to COMPLETED, `results` are stored, and the model appears in the registry — contradicting the cancellation the user was shown and leaving an unwanted model registered.

Severity medium: correctness/UX inconsistency and retained MLflow run for a cancelled job; not a security/data-loss issue.

title: Forecasting endpoints are async but run synchronous MLflow downloads + torch inference, blocking the entire event loop

title: preview_station emits NaN for piezo_std on single-observation series, producing invalid JSON
detail: stats['piezo_std'] = round(float(piezo.std()), 3) is computed unconditionally, before the `if len(piezo) > 1` guard. pandas Series.std() uses ddof=1, so a series with exactly one observation returns NaN. round(float('nan'),3) is still NaN and is placed into the stats dict. Browsers' JSON.parse rejects it, so the /preview call fails on the frontend.

The stats field is typed dict[str, Any] (api/schemas/pastas.py:293) so pydantic does not coerce it, and the /preview route has no response_model. This router does NOT use api.serializers.clean_nans (unlike counterfactual/datasets/forecasting routers, verified via grep). FastAPI's default JSONResponse.render calls json.dumps with allow_nan=True, emitting the bare token NaN — invalid JSON that browsers' JSON.parse rejects, breaking the wizard preview step. title: auto_fit_endpoint runs 4-8 calibrations synchronously with no cancellation, unlike the async pumping pipeline
detail: run_auto_fit executes the full multi-candidate calibration batch (the docstring elsewhere notes 4-8 candidates) inline in the request handler, as does /fit with run_fit. These are sync `def` endpoints, so each occupies a threadpool worker for the entire (potentially minute-scale) calibration with no progress reporting and no way to cancel — in contrast to /pumping-detection/analyze which deliberately offloads to a background thread + SSE stream + stop_event. Under a typical reverse-proxy/gateway idle timeout the client connection is dropped mid-fit while the worker keeps running, and concurrent auto-fits can exhaust the threadpool.

suggested_fix: Offload /fit and /auto-fit to the existing task_manager background-thread + SSE pattern (returning a task_id) so the request returns immediately, progress streams, and stop_event enables cancellation.
verify_reasoning:
Traced the code and confirmed every load-bearing claim.

1) api/routers/pastas.py:1205 `auto_fit_endpoint` is a plain sync `def` (no `async`), and it calls `run_auto_fit(...)` inline (lines 1224-1230), returning only after the whole batch completes. It does NOT pass the available `on_progress` callback (auto_fit.py:141), so there is no progress reporting to the client.

2) run_auto_fit (dashboard/utils/pastas/auto_fit.py:129-317) builds a candidate grid via build_config_grid() and loops over every config calling run_fit() sequentially (line 240, in the per-candidate loop ~227-305). The "4-8 candidates" figure is corroborated by the auto-fit/prune docstring at pastas.py:917 ("4–8 candidates produced by each auto-fit batch"). run_auto_fit has NO stop_event/cancellation parameter — it cannot be interrupted mid-batch.

3) /fit (pastas.py:249) is likewise a sync `def` calling run_fit inline (line 282).

4) The contrast is real: api/routers/pumping_detection.py:84-94 `/analyze` deliberately offloads to `threading.Thread(target=_run_pipeline_thread, daemon=True)` via a task_manager, passes `stop_event=task.stop_event` into pipeline.run (line 68), and exposes an SSE `EventSourceResponse` stream (lines 97-133) for progress + a cancel path. The auto-fit/fit endpoints have none of this.

Since FastAPI runs sync `def` endpoints in the anyio threadpool, each auto-fit occupies a worker for the entire minute-scale batch with no way to cancel. A reverse-proxy idle timeout (e.g. 60s) will drop the client connection while the worker keeps churning through candidates, and the client gets no partial progress and cannot abort — exactly the design inconsistency described.

Severity: medium is appropriate. This is a robustness/perf/UX defect, not a correctness or security bug. One caveat: the "exhaust the threadpool" wording is slightly overstated — FastAPI's default threadpool is 40 workers, so two concurrent users won't literally exhaust it; it takes many concurrent slow fits. But the core verified problems (inline sync multi-calibration, no cancellation, no progress, proxy-timeout dropped connections while work continues) all hold, so the finding stands.

title: ERA5 fallback join uses raw float equality on latitude/longitude, hitting the known coordinate-precision duplicate bug
detail: _load_era5_fallback joins gold.int_era5_for_all_stations to gold.int_station_era5_mapping with `ON m.era5_latitude = e.latitude AND m.era5_longitude = e.longitude`. This is an exact equality on raw floating-point coordinates. The warehouse has a documented ERA5 coordinate-precision bug where the same grid cell is stored with slightly different float representations (backfill vs incremental ingestion). When the mapping table's era5_latitude/longitude differ from the ERA5 data table's latitude/longitude even in the last binary digit, the join yields zero (or partial) rows.
failure_scenario: A piezo station whose inline ERA5 coverage is < 80% (so the code takes the fallback branch) has era5_latitude=48.5 in the mapping table but 48.50000000001 in int_era5_for_all_stations. The equality join returns no rows; era5_df is empty, so load_station_series raises `ValueError: No ERA5 data for station <code>`, and Pastas modelling for that station crashes instead of producing a model. If only a subset of dates were duplicated with drifted floats, the join silently returns a truncated climate series, producing a biased/incomplete forcing for the model.
suggested_fix: Canonicalize coordinates in the join, e.g. `ON ROUND(m.era5_latitude::numeric, 2) = ROUND(e.latitude::numeric, 2) AND ROUND(m.era5_longitude::numeric, 2) = ROUND(e.longitude::numeric, 2)` (matching the grid resolution), or join on a canonical grid-cell id instead of raw floats.
verify_reasoning:
Confirmed the code at dashboard/utils/pastas/station_loader.py:200: _load_era5_fallback joins gold.int_era5_for_all_stations (alias e) to gold.int_station_era5_mapping (alias m) with `ON m.era5_latitude = e.latitude AND m.era5_longitude = e.longitude` — an exact double-precision float equality with no ROUND/canonicalization. If era5_df comes back empty, line 208-209 raises ValueError("No ERA5 data for station ..."), and a partial float match would silently truncate the forcing series (only some duplicated rows join). So the failure MODE described is accurate for the visible app code.

Strong corroborating evidence this is a real anti-pattern in THIS warehouse: api/routers/observatory_era5.py rounds coordinates defensively in ~8 places (`round(latitude::numeric, 1)` in GROUP BY at lines 105-115, 160-167, 343-350, 730-737, 794-801, 866-873, 922-929) precisely to collapse the documented float-duplicate bug. station_loader's fallback join does NOT apply this canonicalization, and there is a suspicious naming asymmetry — the mapping side uses the canonical column `era5_latitude` while the data side uses raw `latitude` (same name as the buggy raw gold.era5_grid table), suggesting the two operands may not share identical float representations. This also violates the stated audit invariant ("flag any join/group-by on raw floats without rounding/canonicalization").

Why PLAUSIBLE and not CONFIRMED: whether the defect actually manifests depends on the dbt intermediate models (int_era5_for_all_stations, int_station_era5_mapping), which live in a SEPARATE repo I cannot inspect. Those int-layer models may already have canonicalized coordinates (the memory notes the fix was applied in dbt silver + re-run), in which case both operands byte-match and equality works. Also note observatory rounds when reading the RAW era5_grid, whereas station_loader reads the derived int_ model, which is more likely to be already cleaned — so real-world impact is uncertain. It only affects the fallback branch (inline coverage < 80% AND < 365 days), narrowing exposure. Corrected severity to medium: real correctness risk with a hard-to-detect silent-truncation mode for affected stations, but data-dependent and possibly already mitigated in the dbt layer. Cheap, safe fix: apply `round(...::numeric, 1)` on both sides of the join (matching the observatory pattern), or key the mapping on canonical coords.

title: Importing dashboard.config for a constant triggers heavy side effects (torch/CUDA init, process-global CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES mutation, filesystem mkdir)
detail: config.py runs real work at import time: it imports torch (line 5), probes CUDA, sets `os.environ['CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES']='0'` and calls `torch.cuda.set_device(0)` (lines 119-123), and creates directories (lines 21-30). Backend code imports this module merely to read constants like MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI (dashboard/utils/mlflow_client.py:36, model_registry.py:106) and plots.py imports it at module top. Additionally the guard at lines 121-122 is ineffective/misleading: `torch.cuda.is_available()` on line 119 already touches the CUDA runtime, so assigning CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES afterward does not re-restrict the current process's torch view (only set_device(0), selecting index 0 among already-visible devices, actually takes effect).

This forces a CUDA context init and pins torch to device 0 process-wide, and mutates the process env var CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES='0' (inherited by any subprocess). On a multi-GPU host where the operator intended another GPU (without pre-setting the env var), work is silently pinned to physical GPU 0; on a driver-less/CPU box the import path does extra CUDA probing for a plain string constant.
suggested_fix: Move device selection and directory creation into explicit init functions (e.g. get_device()/ensure_dirs()) called only by training/inference entrypoints, keep the config module import-time-pure (constants only), and if GPU pinning is desired set CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES before any torch CUDA call (or rely solely on set_device with a clear comment).
verify_reasoning:
Verified dashboard/config.py directly. All factual claims hold: line 5 imports torch at module top; lines 21-30 create directories (mkdir) at import time; lines 119-123 probe CUDA, conditionally set os.environ['CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES']='0' (guarded by `not in os.environ`), and call torch.cuda.set_device(0). These are genuine import-time side effects for a module also used purely for string constants.

The "ineffective/misleading guard" claim is technically correct: torch.cuda.is_available() (line 119) triggers device enumeration (device_count is cached on first call), so assigning CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES afterward (line 122) cannot re-restrict the already-initialized torch CUDA view of the current process — it only affects inherited subprocesses. Only set_device(0) meaningfully takes effect in-process. So the env mutation is dead/misleading for the current process, exactly as claimed.

Tracing callers: model_registry.py:106 (_ensure_tracking_uri) imports dashboard.config UNCONDITIONALLY, and api/routers/forecasting.py:32 imports ModelRegistry — so the backend genuinely reaches this import path. One mitigation the auditor slightly overstated: mlflow_client.py:30-39 (_default_tracking_uri) short-circuits on os.environ['MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI'] BEFORE importing config, and in production Docker that env var is set, so that specific path usually skips the import. Also, in the forecasting path torch is typically already loaded via darts. These reduce but do not eliminate the defect: the model_registry path has no such short-circuit, and the import-time mkdir + process-global CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES='0' + set_device(0) still fire whenever config is imported. On a multi-GPU host where the operator wanted a non-zero GPU without pre-setting the env var, work is silently pinned to physical GPU 0. Defect is real; medium severity (quality/behavioral, no crash/leak) is appropriate.

title: On the /meteo clone, station markers keep the latest classification colour/label when scrubbing the timeline to a past month, contradicting the recoloured sectors.
