title: Frontend SPA is published directly on port 49513, bypassing the hardened reverse-proxy (no security headers, no rate limiting)
detail: The root compose defines a dedicated hardened reverse proxy (service `nginx`, port 49509) that sets X-Frame-Options, CSP, X-Content-Type-Options, HSTS, Permissions-Policy and enforces limit_req rate limiting. But the `frontend` service is ALSO published directly on the host as `${FRONTEND_PORT:-49513}:80`, and its own config `docker/frontend/nginx.conf` contains ZERO security response headers and no rate limiting. Per project memory, the live dib containers (junon-frontend:49513) belong to this root compose project, so real users reach the SPA through 49513 — the unhardened path — rather than 49509.
failure_scenario: A user opens http://10.195.25.16:49513/ (the live junon-frontend). The HTML/index.html is served by docker/frontend/nginx.conf with no X-Frame-Options and no Content-Security-Policy, so the page can be framed by an attacker site (clickjacking of the authenticated app) and no per-IP request throttling applies to /api/ or /. The 49509 reverse proxy that would have added these protections is silently bypassed.
suggested_fix: Do not publish the frontend container to the host in production; expose only the reverse-proxy nginx (49509) and have it proxy the SPA. Alternatively, add the same add_header security block (and limit_req) to docker/frontend/nginx.conf so the directly-exposed front is equally hardened.
verify_reasoning: Traced docker-compose.yml:144 (frontend published ${FRONTEND_PORT:-49513}:80), docker/frontend/Dockerfile:12 (confirms docker/frontend/nginx.conf is the active config via envsubst template), docker/frontend/nginx.conf (no security headers, no limit_req; only gzip, /api/ proxy, SPA try_files), and nginx/nginx.conf (the 49509 reverse proxy that DOES set X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options, Referrer-Policy, HSTS, Permissions-Policy, CSP, and limit_req on /api/ and /). The frontend path is unhardened and published directly on the host. Project memory confirms live dib users reach junon-frontend:49513 and that redeploy rebuilds only backend+frontend (not the nginx proxy), so the hardened 49509 path is bypassed. Clickjacking vector is valid because index.html is served directly by the frontend nginx via try_files, so backend middleware cannot add X-Frame-Options/CSP to the SPA document. Kept medium rather than higher: deployment is HTTP-only on an internal LAN (per COOKIE_SECURE comment), making HSTS moot and limiting exposure to LAN reach, but missing X-Frame-Options/CSP on an authenticated SPA plus absent per-IP throttling on /api/ are genuine gaps.

title: MLflow tracking server is exposed on a host port with no authentication and --allowed-hosts *
detail: MLflow runs with `--host 0.0.0.0 --allowed-hosts *` and is published to the host as `${MLFLOW_PORT:-49512}:5000` in both the root compose (lines 57-66) and deploy/dib-backend/docker-compose.yml (lines 61-70). MLflow ships with no built-in authentication, so anyone who can reach the host on 49512 has full read/write access to the tracking store and can download every logged artifact. README explicitly documents opening http://localhost:49512 for the MLflow UI, confirming it is meant to be reachable.
failure_scenario: On the shared university LAN, any host reaches http://10.195.25.16:49512/ and, with no credentials, browses experiments, downloads model artifacts (potentially derived from sensitive piezo/BRGM data), deletes runs, or registers malicious model versions. There is no auth gate and --allowed-hosts * disables the DNS-rebinding host check.
suggested_fix: Do not publish MLflow to the host in production; keep it on the internal compose network only (drop the `ports:` mapping) and reach it via the backend, or front it with an authenticating reverse proxy and restrict --allowed-hosts to the known host(s).
verify_reasoning: Verified docker-compose.yml lines 57-66: MLflow (ghcr.io/mlflow/mlflow:v3.8.1) publishes `${MLFLOW_PORT:-49512}:5000` (no host-IP bind, so it binds 0.0.0.0 on the host and is reachable on the LAN) and its command runs `mlflow server --host 0.0.0.0 ... --allowed-hosts *`. deploy/dib-backend/docker-compose.yml lines 61-70 are identical. Grep for MLFLOW_TRACKING_USERNAME/PASSWORD/basic_auth/auth across both compose files and deploy/ returns nothing — no authentication layer, no reverse-proxy auth, no bind to 127.0.0.1. MLflow open-source ships with no built-in auth by default, and --allowed-hosts * disables the DNS-rebinding host check. README.md line 68 and 122 confirm the UI is meant to be opened at http://localhost:49512. MEMORY notes the host is on the university LAN at 10.195.25.16. So any host on that LAN can reach http://10.195.25.16:49512/ and browse experiments, download model artifacts (derived from piezo/BRGM data), delete runs, or register malicious model versions — no credential gate. The defect and failure scenario hold exactly as described. Severity medium is appropriate: real unauthenticated exposure but limited to LAN reach and data is hydrogeology/model artifacts rather than credentials or personal data; not internet-exposed. Suggested fix: bind to 127.0.0.1 (e.g. `127.0.0.1:${MLFLOW_PORT:-49512}:5000`) or drop the host port entirely (backend already reaches it via the internal `http://mlflow:5000`), and/or front it with an authenticating reverse proxy; tighten --allowed-hosts to the intended hostname.

title: Startup warms four full-table scans where the temp/precip climatology scans duplicate data already produced by the STI/SPI warmers
detail: On startup (api/main.py:94-97) four ~130s full-table scans of gold.era5_grid run: _era5_temp_climatology (temperature per cell/month, 1991-2020, line 216), _era5_precip_climatology (precip per cell/month, 1991-2020, line 268), _warm_era5_sti_default (temperature per cell/year/month, 1990-2021, line 647) and _warm_era5_spi_default (precip per cell/year/month, 1990-2021, line 672). The STI/SPI warmers already build per-(cell, year, month) means/sums in `by_cell`; the climatology outputs (per-(cell, calendar-month) mean over years) are derivable from that same in-memory structure. The recent perf commit collapsed 48 reference scans into one per variable, but two of the four remaining full scans re-read the same columns over an overlapping period.
failure_scenario: Every cold start / cache-refresh path (main.py:134-137) pays ~2 redundant full scans (~4-5 min extra) reading the same temperature and precipitation columns already streamed by the STI/SPI warmers.
suggested_fix: Derive the temp and precip climatologies from the STI/SPI warmers' `by_cell` maps (average the per-year monthly values over 1991-2020) and cache them there, removing the two standalone full-table climatology scans; or share a single scan per variable feeding both climatology and references.
verify_reasoning: Read observatory_era5.py lines 199-311 and 565-691 plus main.py:84-149. Confirmed: on startup main.py:93-98 warms four full-table scans of gold.era5_grid. _era5_temp_climatology (line 216) scans temperature_2m over 1991-2020 grouped by (lat,lon,calendar-month); _warm_era5_sti_default (line 647) scans the SAME column temperature_2m over the SUPERSET period 1990-2020 at (lat,lon,year,month) grain — its per-(year,month) means aggregate up to the climatology's per-calendar-month mean. Same pairing holds for total_precipitation between _era5_precip_climatology (line 268) and _warm_era5_spi_default (line 672). So two of the four scans genuinely re-read the same columns over an overlapping period the STI/SPI scans already stream; the redundancy is real and the climatology output is derivable from the same scan. Two caveats keep this at low: (1) exact climatology needs per-(year,month) counts for weighting, which _scan_monthly_cell_stats computes (sn) but discards when building by_cell at line 590-591 — so derivation needs the scan's counts retained, not by_cell as-is; still trivially achievable. (2) The failure scenario's '~4-5 min extra' is overstated: the four scans run concurrently via asyncio.gather/to_thread, so the real cost is extra parallel DB I/O contention (4 scans vs a possible 2), not additive minutes. Core claim of duplicated scans is accurate; it is a valid perf/low optimization opportunity, not a correctness bug.

title: /snapshot crashes with TypeError on an empty grid table because it does not guard the None max-date like the other endpoints
detail: In get_era5_snapshot, when `date` is omitted, `d` is set from `SELECT max("time")::date` (line 101-103). If gold.era5_grid is empty, `.scalar()` returns None, and line 117 then evaluates `d + timedelta(days=1)`, raising TypeError -> 500. Every other endpoint that resolves the max date guards it (`_resolve_month_start` returns None on empty table, line 324; /range reads min/max but returns strings). This endpoint is the lone one missing the guard, so it is an inconsistency rather than intentional.
failure_scenario: GET /api/v1/observatory/era5/snapshot with no date against an empty or freshly-truncated gold.era5_grid -> `None + timedelta(days=1)` -> unhandled TypeError -> HTTP 500 instead of an empty result.
suggested_fix: After resolving `d`, add `if d is None: return []` before building the query (mirroring the month_start None-guards in the other endpoints).
verify_reasoning: Traced the code in api/routers/observatory_era5.py get_era5_snapshot. When the `date` query param is omitted, `d = snapshot_date` is None, so lines 100-103 execute `SELECT max("time")::date FROM gold.era5_grid` and set d via `.scalar()`. On an empty/truncated gold.era5_grid, `max()` yields NULL and `.scalar()` returns None. Line 117 then unconditionally evaluates `d + timedelta(days=1)`, i.e. `None + timedelta(...)`, raising TypeError. This exception is not caught: get_cached (dashboard/utils/cache.py:103) calls fetch_fn() with no try/except around it (only the surrounding Redis get/setex are guarded), so the TypeError propagates to FastAPI -> HTTP 500 instead of an empty result. No upstream guard exists: snapshot_date is Optional and defaults to None, and there is no None-check between line 103 and 117. The claim that other endpoints guard is corroborated (the monthly path uses _resolve_month_start which can short-circuit). Severity is correctly low: it only triggers on an empty/freshly-truncated table (not the normal populated state), and the impact is a 500 rather than a graceful empty list — an inconsistency/robustness bug, not a data-correctness or security issue. Suggested fix: after resolving d, `if d is None: return []` before computing d_next.

title: parse_brgm_sectors filters to a single global latest end_period, silently dropping any sector whose most recent published window lags behind
detail: parse_brgm_sectors computes `latest = max(end_periods)` across ALL parent features and then keeps only features whose end_period == latest (lines 39-42). This assumes every sector shares the exact same most-recent end_period. If BRGM publishes windows non-uniformly (a sector updated on a different 15-day cadence, or one sector missing from the newest bulletin), that sector's end_period is strictly less than the global max and it is dropped from the /brgm-sectors output entirely — the sector loses its class/color/trend rather than falling back to its own latest window. Notably parse_brgm_timeline in the same file handles this correctly by tracking best[month][sector_id] per sector, showing the author knows per-sector granularity is required.
failure_scenario: WFS returns sector A with end_period=2026-06-15 and sector B with end_period=2026-05-31 (B not in the newest bulletin). latest=2026-06-15, so B is filtered out and never appears in the returned list; the observatory map shows no BRGM class/trend for sector B even though a valid recent window exists.
suggested_fix: Instead of a global max filter, keep the latest window per sector_id (mirror parse_brgm_timeline: group by sector_id and pick max end_period within each group), then dedup.
verify_reasoning: Read api/routers/observatory_meteo.py lines 22-120. Lines 39-42 of parse_brgm_sectors compute a single global latest = max(end_periods) across ALL parent features, then keep only features where end_period == latest. This is a global collapse with no per-sector fallback: any sector whose most-recent published window lags behind the global maximum is dropped entirely and loses its class/color/trend in the /brgm-sectors output. The contrast with parse_brgm_timeline (lines 108+), which tracks best[month][sector_id] per sector, confirms per-sector granularity is both required and achievable, so the global filter is a genuine divergence rather than an intentional invariant. The code logic matches the finding exactly. The only uncertainty is data-dependent: manifesting the bug requires the WFS to return non-uniform end_periods across sectors (e.g. a sector missing from the newest bulletin). The BRGM national bulletin is usually uniform per publication, so real-world impact is likely rare — hence low severity is appropriate. A safe fix: track the latest end_period per sector_id (like parse_brgm_timeline) instead of a single global max.

title: Login is vulnerable to user-enumeration via a response-timing side channel
detail: The login check `user is None or not user.is_active or not verify_password(req.password, user.password_hash)` short-circuits: when the submitted email does not exist (or the account is inactive), `verify_password` is never called, so the expensive Argon2 hash verification is skipped. `api/auth/passwords.py` uses `PasswordHash.recommended()` (Argon2), which takes tens of milliseconds. This creates a measurable timing gap between 'no such user' (fast, no hashing) and 'user exists, wrong password' (slow, full hash verify). The scope module `passwords.py` also exposes no constant-time dummy-verify helper to equalize timing.
failure_scenario: An attacker submits POST /api/v1/auth/login for candidate emails with a bogus password. Requests for registered emails consistently take ~50-100ms longer (Argon2 verify) than requests for unknown emails (immediate 401). By measuring latency the attacker enumerates which emails have accounts, then focuses brute-force/lockout-evasion on real accounts.
suggested_fix: Always perform a hash verification against a fixed dummy Argon2 hash when the user is missing/inactive, so every login path executes one verify. E.g. add `verify_dummy()` in passwords.py that verifies against a precomputed hash, and call it in the `user is None` branch; keep the final decision constant-time.
verify_reasoning: Traced api/routers/auth.py:52 and api/auth/passwords.py. The condition `user is None or not user.is_active or not verify_password(req.password, user.password_hash)` uses Python's left-to-right short-circuit `or`. If `user is None` (unknown email) or `not user.is_active` (inactive account), evaluation stops before `verify_password` is called, so the Argon2 KDF (pwdlib.PasswordHash.recommended() -> Argon2, tens of ms) runs ONLY when an active user exists. passwords.py exposes only hash_password/verify_password — no constant-time dummy-verify helper to equalize the missing branch, confirming the claimed absence of mitigation. So the code defect (timing gap between 'active user, wrong password' = slow and 'unknown/inactive account' = fast) is real, and the described enumeration scenario is mechanically valid. Adversarial checks that could refute it: (1) both branches also run register_failure + record_event + db.commit, but that shared work is present in ALL failing paths and does not mask the extra Argon2 cost that appears only for existing active users; (2) enforce_ip_rate_limit and is_locked run first, which throttle but do not eliminate the differential; (3) is_locked returns 429 before the DB query, but that only affects already-locked emails. None of these remove the timing asymmetry — they only add noise. I lowered severity from medium to low: this is a network-observable side channel requiring statistical sampling against jitter, and IP rate limiting plus a generic 'Identifiants invalides' message reduce practical exploitability; it leaks account existence, not credentials. Recommended fix: always call verify_password against a fixed precomputed dummy Argon2 hash when the user is missing/inactive (or use pwdlib's dummy-verify pattern) so every path performs one Argon2 verification.

title: Logout does not invalidate the session token server-side
detail: Session tokens are stateless JWTs (api/auth/tokens.py) validated in deps.py only by signature, expiry, and `token_version` equality. `change_password` correctly increments `user.token_version` to revoke existing sessions, but `logout` (auth.py:71-73) merely calls `response.delete_cookie` and never bumps `token_version`. Any copy of the JWT that existed before logout therefore remains fully valid until its `exp` (session_ttl_hours = 12h).
failure_scenario: A user logs out on a shared/public machine, or a token was captured (e.g. via prior network interception or a browser extension). After logout the stolen cookie value still authenticates every endpoint via get_current_user until the 12h expiry, because token_version is unchanged — logout gives a false sense of session termination.
suggested_fix: Either make logout increment `user.token_version` (and commit) to revoke the token like change_password does, or maintain a server-side session/denylist keyed by a jti claim so logged-out tokens are rejected before expiry.
verify_reasoning: Traced the full auth flow. api/routers/auth.py:71-73 logout() takes only Response, calls response.delete_cookie() and nothing else — it has no db dependency and never increments token_version. Sessions are stateless JWTs (api/auth/tokens.py: create_session_token embeds sub/tv/iat/exp; decode_session_token only verifies signature+expiry). api/auth/deps.py:20-28 authenticates by decoding the JWT and checking user.is_active and user.token_version == tv against the DB — there is no server-side session/denylist. The only revocation lever is token_version, which change_password (auth.py:92) correctly bumps but logout does not. Therefore a copy of the pre-logout cookie value still authenticates every get_current_user endpoint until exp (session_ttl_hours = 12h per project memory). The failure scenario (shared machine / captured token still valid post-logout) holds exactly as claimed. Severity kept at low: exploitation requires the attacker to already possess the token, the cookie is httponly and is cleared client-side, and stateless-JWT logout-without-revocation is a well-understood design tradeoff with bounded 12h exposure rather than an unauthenticated break.

title: create_admin.py accepts the admin password as a plaintext CLI argument, exposing it via shell history and the process table
detail: The --password option (line 19, used at line 22) lets the full admin credential be passed on the command line. On a shared host this value is visible to any user via `ps`/`/proc/<pid>/cmdline` while the script runs and is written to the invoking shell's history file. The script already supports a secure getpass prompt when --password is omitted, so the plaintext argument path is an avoidable credential-leak vector for the highest-privilege account.
failure_scenario: Operator runs `python scripts/create_admin.py --email a@b.fr --name X --password S3cret!` inside the backend container. Another process/user runs `ps aux ww` during execution and captures the admin password; it also persists in ~/.bash_history.
suggested_fix: Drop the --password argument (or accept the secret only via an environment variable / stdin) and always use getpass; if kept for automation, document that it must come from a file/env, never an inline literal.
verify_reasoning: Read scripts/create_admin.py in full. The `--password` optional argument is defined on line 20 (the finding says line 19, which is actually `--name` — minor anchor error) and consumed on line 22: `password = args.password or getpass.getpass("Password: ")`. When invoked as `--password S3cret!`, the plaintext admin credential is placed in the process argv, exposed to any local user via `ps aux ww` / `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` for the script's runtime, and persisted to the invoking shell's history file. This is the highest-privilege account (role=UserRole.admin). A secure getpass prompt path already exists (taken when --password is omitted), so the plaintext-arg path is an avoidable leak vector. The described failure scenario is reproducible as written. Severity low is correct: exploitation needs a co-located local user racing a short-lived process and a safe alternative is built in; a real but low-impact hygiene defect. Verdict CONFIRMED despite the off-by-one line number, since the defect and scenario are real.

title: ips_reference loads the reference grid and then discards it, re-querying the same table a second time
detail: ips_reference calls _load_station_grid(entry.station_name) at line 610 (which creates a SQLAlchemy engine, opens a connection, SELECTs month/quantile_grid from gold.station_reference_stats, then disposes the engine). The returned `station_grid` is never referenced again. Immediately after (lines 618-632) the handler builds ANOTHER engine and runs essentially the same SELECT (month, quantile_grid, n_years) on the same table for the same station. So each /ips-reference request pays for two engine constructions, two connections, and two near-identical queries where one would do.
failure_scenario: Every GET /api/v1/counterfactual/ips-reference does 2x the DB round-trips and 2x engine/pool creation; under a dashboard that polls this per model the redundant work doubles DB load for zero benefit.
suggested_fix: Delete the unused line 610 call and derive n_years/mu/sigma from the single query at 618-632 (or extend _load_station_grid to also return n_years and reuse its result).
verify_reasoning: Verified in api/routers/counterfactual.py. Line 610 assigns station_grid = _load_station_grid(entry.station_name); _load_station_grid (def at line 49) builds a fresh engine, opens a connection, SELECTs month/quantile_grid from gold.station_reference_stats for the station, and disposes the engine. That station_grid is never referenced anywhere in the ips_reference handler (lines 610-658). Lines 618-632 then construct a SECOND engine and run essentially the same query (adds only n_years), and its meta_rows are what actually build ref_stats_for_window and n_years. So every GET /ips-reference does a redundant engine construction + connection + query whose result is discarded; the second query is a strict superset, so the first is pure dead work. (For contrast, the CF thread at line 124 stores the grid as _station_grid and genuinely uses it at line 304, so the pattern is clearly a copy-paste leftover here.) The failure scenario holds: 2x engine/pool creation and 2x round-trips per request. I set severity to low rather than the claimed medium: it is a single wasted query on an auth-gated GET endpoint, not a demonstrated hot path, and the endpoint recreates engines per call regardless; the fix is trivial (drop line 610 or reuse its result).

title: A fresh SQLAlchemy engine (with its own connection pool) is created and disposed on every warehouse read
detail: _load_station_grid (line 56), ips_reference (line 618) and ips_bounds (via _load_station_grid) each call create_engine(_brgm_url()) then engine.dispose() per invocation. create_engine builds a new QueuePool and a brand-new DB connection each time, defeating connection pooling; engines are intended to be long-lived/module-level. In the CF background thread and the IPS endpoints this means a new TCP+auth handshake to brgm-postgres on every request.
failure_scenario: Bursts of /ips-bounds, /ips-reference and CF runs each open a fresh Postgres connection and tear it down, adding connection-setup latency and pressure on the warehouse's max_connections instead of reusing a pooled engine.
suggested_fix: Create one module-level engine (lazily, from _brgm_url()) and reuse it via `with engine.connect()`; do not dispose it per call.
verify_reasoning:
I read counterfactual.py and confirmed the exact pattern. `_load_station_grid` (line 56) does `engine = create_engine(_brgm_url())` then `engine.dispose()` (line 71) per call; `ips_reference` does the same (create at 618, dispose at 632). `ips_bounds` calls `_load_station_grid`, inheriting the pattern. `_run_cf_thread` (the CF background thread) also computes IPS bounds via these helpers. create_engine builds a fresh QueuePool; engine.connect() opens a new TCP+auth handshake to the external brgm-postgres each call, and dispose() tears the whole pool down, so no pooling/reuse ever occurs.

The finding is corroborated decisively by api/database.py:48-69, which provides a lazily-created, module-level, pooled `get_brgm_sync_engine()` (pool_size=5, max_overflow=10, pool_pre_ping, pool_recycle=3600) with a comment (lines 50-51) explicitly stating: "Reuse this instead of create_engine() per request, which paid a new-connection setup to the external warehouse each call." Other routers (observatory_common.py, observatory_era5.py) correctly use this helper; counterfactual.py (and pastas.py) bypass it. So the intended pattern exists in-repo and counterfactual.py violates it — the defect is real and the failure scenario (per-request connection setup latency + max_connections pressure on the warehouse under bursts) holds.

Severity stays low: these are model-owner-gated, low-frequency endpoints (IPS reference/bounds, CF runs), not hot paths, so impact is connection-setup latency and warehouse connection churn rather than a correctness or availability bug. Fix: replace the per-call create_engine/dispose in _load_station_grid and ips_reference with api.database.get_brgm_sync_engine() and drop the dispose() calls.

title: get_layer_result can never serve partial layers before completion, defeating progressive rendering
detail: In pumping_detection.py the endpoint's docstring promises 'progressive rendering', and it returns task.result[layer_name] only if `task.result and layer_name in task.result`. But _run_pipeline_thread assigns task.result exactly once, at the very end (line 71), inside the COMPLETED transition; task.result is None (TaskInfo.result defaults to None) for the entire duration of the run. Partial state is written only to the metrics file via emit(), never to task.result. Therefore /layer/{name} returns 404 'not yet available' for every layer until the whole pipeline finishes, at which point /results already returns everything — so the endpoint offers no progressive benefit.
failure_scenario: Client starts analysis, then polls GET /api/v1/pumping-detection/{task_id}/layer/pastas while the pipeline is still on the changepoints stage -> always 404 until the entire pipeline COMPLETES, so incremental UI rendering per-layer is impossible.
suggested_fix: Have the pipeline populate task.result incrementally (under task.lock) as each layer finishes, or change the layer endpoint to read completed layers from the metrics file instead of task.result.
verify_reasoning: Traced the full chain. TaskInfo.result defaults to None (api/task_manager.py:29). In _run_pipeline_thread (api/routers/pumping_detection.py:26-81), task.result is assigned exactly once, at line 71, inside the with-lock block that sets TaskStatus.COMPLETED. The pipeline (PumpingDetectionPipeline.run) is given only the emit callback and has no reference to the TaskInfo object; emit (lines 38-44) writes partial state to the metrics JSON file via json.dump, overwriting each time. Confirmed via grep that the ONLY assignment to task.result in this router is line 71; partial stages (pipeline.py lines 54,73,94, etc.) only call self.emit(...) to the metrics file. Therefore get_layer_result (line 148-162) evaluates `if not task.result or layer_name not in task.result` -> task.result is None for the entire RUNNING duration -> raises HTTPException(404, "Layer '{name}' not yet available") for every layer until the pipeline completes. Once COMPLETED, /results (line 136-145) already returns the full dict, so the layer endpoint gives no progressive benefit — the actual progressive channel is the SSE /stream endpoint (reads metrics file, surfaces partial_result). The failure scenario (poll /layer/pastas during the changepoints stage -> always 404 until COMPLETED) holds exactly. One header inaccuracy: the finding lists FILE as api/routers/pastas.py:160, but the code is in api/routers/pumping_detection.py:160 (the DETAIL correctly names pumping_detection.py). Severity low is correct: no crash/leak/wrong-science; the docstring's 'enables progressive rendering' promise is simply unfulfilled and the endpoint is effectively redundant/dead for its stated purpose.

title: export_pas leaks the temp .pas file if model.to_file fails
detail: A NamedTemporaryFile is created with delete=False and only unlinked via the BackgroundTask attached to the successful FileResponse. If model.to_file(f.name) raises (e.g. serialization error, disk full), the exception propagates before FileResponse is constructed, so the BackgroundTask is never registered and the zero/partial-byte temp file is left on disk permanently. Repeated failures accumulate orphaned files in the temp dir.
failure_scenario: GET /api/v1/pastas/models/{run_id}/export/pas where model.to_file raises -> 500 response and an orphaned /tmp/*.pas file that is never cleaned up; repeated calls slowly fill the temp filesystem.
suggested_fix: Wrap to_file in try/except and os.unlink(f.name) on failure before re-raising (or write into a TemporaryDirectory cleaned in a finally).
verify_reasoning: Read api/routers/pastas.py:816-838. Confirmed the exact structure the finding describes. Line 830: `f = tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(suffix=".pas", delete=False)`; 831 closes it (creating a zero-byte file on disk); 832 `model.to_file(f.name)`; and only at 833-838 is the FileResponse built with `background=BackgroundTask(os.unlink, f.name)`. Because delete=False, the OS will not auto-remove the file when the handle is closed/GC'd. The sole cleanup path is the BackgroundTask, which is only registered once FileResponse is successfully constructed. If model.to_file raises (serialization error, disk full, permissions), the exception propagates out of the endpoint (becoming a 500) before FileResponse exists, so no BackgroundTask is scheduled and the zero/partial-byte temp file is orphaned in the temp dir. There is no try/finally or try/except around lines 830-832 to unlink on failure. Repeated failures accumulate orphaned files. The failure scenario holds exactly as claimed. Severity low is correct: it is a resource/quality leak only triggered on the error path, not a security or correctness issue in normal operation, and each orphan is small. Suggested fix: wrap to_file in try/except that os.unlink(f.name) and re-raises (or use try/finally with a success flag), so the temp file is removed when serialization fails.

title: asfreq('D') regularization loop in _load_era5_fallback is a no-op; returned ERA5 series keep irregular frequency
detail: The loop `for s in (precip, evap, temp): if s.index.freq is None: s = s.asfreq('D')` rebinds the loop-local variable `s` but never writes back to precip/evap/temp, so the reassignment is discarded. The three Series returned to load_station_series are therefore never resampled to a regular daily index. This contrasts with the inline branch, which passes every series through _regularize() (asfreq('D') + interpolate + edge trim). The fallback path thus returns climate series that may have gaps / missing dates and no set frequency.
failure_scenario: A station taking the ERA5-fallback branch returns precip/evap/temp with an irregular DatetimeIndex (freq=None, missing days). Downstream Pastas stress construction (which assumes an equally-spaced daily series) either raises on the irregular index or silently misaligns the stress with the piezo head, yielding a wrong recharge model — and the inconsistency vs the inline branch means two stations with identical data can produce different models depending only on whether inline coverage crossed 80%.
suggested_fix: Regularize each series and reassign, e.g. build a list `out = [_regularize(precip), _regularize(evap), _regularize(temp)]` (reusing the same helper as the inline branch) and `return out[0], out[1], out[2]`, instead of the ineffective in-loop `s = s.asfreq('D')`.
verify_reasoning: CONFIRMED at code level: dashboard/utils/pastas/station_loader.py:218-220 — `for s in (precip, evap, temp): if s.index.freq is None: s = s.asfreq("D")` rebinds the loop-local `s` and never writes back; asfreq returns a new object and does not mutate, so the returned tuple (line 222) is the original series with .freq still None. This is genuinely inconsistent with the inline branch (lines 169-172) which uses _regularize(). However, the claimed FAILURE SCENARIO (Pastas crash / misaligned stress / divergent models) is not substantiated: (1) the fallback source gold.int_era5_for_all_stations is gapless daily ERA5 reanalysis, so after set_index/sort/dedup the index is a regular daily DatetimeIndex — only the .freq attribute is unset, dates are not actually missing; (2) ps.RechargeModel (builder.py:68) / Pastas TimeSeries infer the frequency from the DatetimeIndex via pd.infer_freq, which returns 'D' for gapless daily data, so no raise or misalignment; (3) _validate_series (builder.py:20-41) never inspects .freq; (4) even a working asfreq('D') would be a no-op on gapless data and would only insert NaNs (which Pastas rejects) if gaps existed. The bug is thus mostly harmless dead code that fails to match the inline branch's contract. It could only bite if the ERA5 fallback series actually contained date gaps (e.g. via the known float-coordinate join dropping rows), which is data-dependent and I could not confirm — hence PLAUSIBLE, low severity, not the medium/crash impact claimed.

title: Streamlit config files are orphaned and never applied (wrong filename + no Streamlit entrypoint)
detail: Streamlit only auto-loads a file literally named `.streamlit/config.toml` (or `~/.streamlit/config.toml`, or a path passed via STREAMLIT_* env). These files are named `config_explorer.toml` and `config_training.toml`, and a repo-wide search shows (a) nothing references them (no `streamlit run`, no Dockerfile/compose/Makefile/shell script copies or symlinks them, no `--config`), and (b) no module under dashboard/ imports streamlit or calls st.set_page_config — the app has migrated to FastAPI+React. So the server hardening/theme settings here (maxUploadSize, enableXsrfProtection, enableCORS, theme) are dead config: they are silently ignored.
failure_scenario: An operator edits config_training.toml to set enableXsrfProtection=true / maxUploadSize=500 believing they harden or tune a running Streamlit app; because the file is never loaded (wrong name, no live Streamlit process), the settings have zero effect and give a false sense of configuration.
suggested_fix: If Streamlit is truly retired, delete the dashboard/.streamlit/ directory to avoid misleading dead config. If a Streamlit app is still meant to run, rename to `.streamlit/config.toml` (only one can exist) or launch with an explicit config path / STREAMLIT_* env vars, and add the launch command to the Dockerfile/compose.
verify_reasoning: Traced the claim directly. dashboard/.streamlit/ contains only config_explorer.toml and config_training.toml (line 8+ hold [server] maxUploadSize/enableCORS/enableXsrfProtection). Streamlit only auto-loads a file literally named .streamlit/config.toml (or ~/.streamlit/config.toml, or a path via STREAMLIT_* env / --config). Repo-wide greps confirm: (a) no file named config.toml exists anywhere; (b) zero `import streamlit`/`from streamlit` statements and no st.set_page_config anywhere; (c) no `streamlit run` and no `--config` in any Dockerfile/compose/Makefile/shell script; (d) the only STREAMLIT_ reference is robust_loader.py toggling STREAMLIT_RUNTIME_EXISTS defensively, which does not load config. A plan doc (2026-06-05-pr2-streamlit-removal.md) confirms the app migrated off Streamlit to FastAPI+React, and mentions of 'Streamlit' elsewhere are comments/docs only. Therefore these settings are never loaded and are silently ignored; the failure scenario (an operator editing enableXsrfProtection/maxUploadSize believing it hardens/tunes a running app, with zero effect) holds. Defect is real. I downgrade severity from medium to low: it is purely orphaned dead config with no live process to affect, so real-world impact is limited to operator confusion rather than an exploitable security/functional regression. Suggested fix: delete both files (dead config) or, if a Streamlit tool is still intended, rename to config.toml and wire an entrypoint; otherwise remove to avoid the false sense of hardening.

title: MODEL_COLORS / MODELS cover only 4 of the 12 supported architectures
detail: config.py defines MODELS=['NBEATS','TFT','TCN','LSTM'] and MODEL_COLORS for only those four, but models_config.py/ModelFactory support 12 DL architectures (NHiTS, Transformer, GRU, BlockRNN, TiDE, DLinear, NLinear, TSMixer, ...). plots.py uses MODEL_COLORS.get(model,'gray') so it does not crash, but every model outside the four renders in the same fallback 'gray', making multi-model comparison charts ambiguous.
failure_scenario: A comparison plot including NHiTS and TSMixer (both common/recommended) draws both series in identical gray, so they are visually indistinguishable in the legend/curves.
suggested_fix: Derive colors from the full model list in models_config.py (e.g. assign a stable palette over ALL_MODELS keys) instead of a hardcoded 4-entry dict, or explicitly add distinct colors for all supported architectures.

RECOMMENDED_MODELS explicitly lists NHiTS and TSMixer, neither of which has a color. dashboard/utils/plots.py uses MODEL_COLORS.get(model, 'gray') at lines 359 (plot_forecast_comparison curves), 401 (bar chart), and 465 (radar), so there is no crash, but every model outside the 4 renders in the same fallback gray. Suggested fix: extend MODEL_COLORS to cover all keys in ALL_MODELS (or derive colors programmatically, e.g. from a Plotly qualitative palette keyed on model name) so every architecture gets a distinct color.

title: Query-string parameters interpolated without encodeURIComponent in several api.ts calls (inconsistent with pastas' own encoding)
detail: db.tables/columns/distinct/dateRange (lines 142-155) and pastas.models (line 300, `?code_bss=${codeBss}`) build query strings by raw template interpolation, whereas pastas.stationInfo/siblings/preview/fit correctly use encodeURIComponent(codeBss) and db.searchStations uses URLSearchParams. Any value containing '&', '#', '+', or spaces will corrupt the URL (a '+' decodes to space server-side, '&' injects a spurious param, '#' truncates). BSS codes and warehouse identifiers are generally clean, so impact is limited, but the inconsistency is a latent correctness bug.
failure_scenario: pastas.models is called with a code_bss containing '+' or '&' (or a schema/column name with a space passed to db.columns); the resulting request drops or misinterprets the parameter and the backend query returns wrong/empty results.
suggested_fix: Wrap every interpolated query value in encodeURIComponent, matching the rest of the pastas API surface, or build all query strings with URLSearchParams.
verify_reasoning: Verified frontend/src/lib/api.ts directly. Line 300 (pastas.models) uses raw template interpolation `?code_bss=${codeBss}` with no encoding, whereas the sibling pastas methods stationInfo (281), siblings (285), preview (286) and fit-adjacent code all use encodeURIComponent(codeBss), and db.searchStations (162-169) uses URLSearchParams. db.tables (143), db.columns (149), db.distinct (151), db.dateRange (154) likewise interpolate schema/table/column raw. The inconsistency and missing URL-encoding are exactly as described. The failure scenario (a value with '&','#','+', or space corrupting the query string — '+' → space, '&' → spurious param, '#' → truncation) is mechanically correct. Practical reachability is low: code_bss values here are the alphanumeric BSS designation format and DB identifiers are [a-z0-9_], so the offending characters essentially never appear — which matches the claimed 'low' severity and the finding's own acknowledgment of limited impact. Defect is real code (not a misread), framework does not auto-encode raw template strings, so the claim stands. Fix: use encodeURIComponent for code_bss and route the db.* identifiers through URLSearchParams for consistency.

title: nginx add_header in /assets/ and /observatory-bridge.js blocks inheritance of the server-level security headers
detail: nginx only inherits `add_header` directives into a location if that location defines NO add_header of its own. In deploy/frontend/nginx.conf.template the `location /assets/` block (lines 64-67) adds Cache-Control, and `location = /observatory-bridge.js` (lines 56-61) adds three headers; both therefore drop all the server-level security headers (X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options, Referrer-Policy, HSTS, Permissions-Policy, CSP) for those responses. The same pattern exists in nginx/nginx.conf (observatory-bridge location, lines 52-57).
failure_scenario: A response for /assets/index-*.js or /observatory-bridge.js is returned without X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and without the CSP set at server level, so those script/asset responses lack the MIME-sniffing and content-security protections applied to the rest of the site.
suggested_fix: Re-declare the required security add_header directives inside these location blocks, or move common headers to a shared include and repeat it wherever a location introduces its own add_header (nginx has no additive inheritance).
verify_reasoning: Read deploy/frontend/nginx.conf.template and nginx/nginx.conf. nginx's documented rule: add_header directives are inherited into a location only if that location defines NO add_header of its own. location = /observatory-bridge.js (lines 56-61) defines Content-Type/Cache-Control/Access-Control-Allow-Origin, and location /assets/ (lines 64-67) defines Cache-Control; both therefore suppress inheritance of the six server-level security headers declared at lines 31-36 (X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options, Referrer-Policy, HSTS, Permissions-Policy, CSP). Same pattern confirmed in nginx/nginx.conf lines 52-57. So responses for /assets/* and /observatory-bridge.js are served without those headers — the finding's mechanism and failure scenario hold. Severity correctly low, arguably even lower in practical impact: most dropped headers are inert on a subresource/script response (CSP is enforced from the loading document, not the script response; X-Frame-Options/Referrer-Policy matter only for documents; HSTS is already set by index.html). The only header with meaningful value here is X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff on JS assets. Defect is real; keep low.

title: Conflicting/stale mlflow pins across pyproject, base.txt, requirements.txt and uv.lock
detail: There are four dependency sources with three different mlflow constraints: requirements/base.txt line 36 requires mlflow>=3.9.0; pyproject.toml line 56 requires mlflow>=3.8.0; the committed compiled requirements.txt line 227 pins mlflow==3.8.1; and uv.lock pins mlflow==3.9.0. The compiled requirements.txt (mlflow==3.8.1) does NOT satisfy requirements/base.txt's >=3.9.0 floor and is out of sync with uv.lock (3.9.0), so the repo ships two mutually inconsistent lockfiles.
failure_scenario: CI/dev installs via `pip install -r requirements.txt` -> gets mlflow 3.8.1; another path installs via `pip install -r requirements/base.txt` or `uv sync` -> gets mlflow 3.9.0. The two environments diverge, and anything relying on mlflow>=3.9.0 (as base.txt declares) silently runs on 3.8.1 when the compiled file is used, producing non-reproducible / version-skewed builds.
suggested_fix: Recompile requirements.txt from the current pyproject/uv.lock (`uv pip compile pyproject.toml -o requirements.txt`) so mlflow==3.9.0, and reconcile the floor: set pyproject.toml and requirements/base.txt to the same minimum (e.g. mlflow>=3.9.0). Ideally drop the hand-maintained requirements/*.txt duplicates in favor of uv.lock as the single source of truth.
verify_reasoning: All four numeric facts verified: requirements/base.txt:36 = mlflow>=3.9.0; pyproject.toml:56 = mlflow>=3.8.0 (plus unpinned "mlflow" at line 20); requirements.txt:227 = mlflow==3.8.1 (also mlflow-skinny/tracing==3.8.1); uv.lock line 1332 = mlflow 3.9.0. Three distinct constraints across four sources genuinely exist, so the "conflicting/stale pins" defect is real — CONFIRMED. However the finding's framing is partly wrong on two points, which lowers severity: (1) requirements.txt's own header states it is compiled from pyproject.toml (uv pip compile pyproject.toml -o requirements.txt), NOT from base.txt — so 3.8.1 DOES satisfy its true source (>=3.8.0); the genuine defect is that requirements.txt is stale relative to uv.lock (both derive from pyproject.toml yet disagree, 3.8.1 vs 3.9.0). (2) The failure scenario asserts CI/dev install via `pip install -r requirements.txt` and `pip install -r requirements/base.txt`, but grepping all Dockerfiles/CI/compose shows NEITHER file is referenced by any automated build: docker/backend/Dockerfile uses `pip install ".[api,cuda|cpu]"` (pyproject) and .github/workflows/test.yml uses `uv sync --extra cpu --extra api` (uv.lock -> 3.9.0). Both real paths converge on 3.9.0, so actual builds do not diverge. requirements.txt and requirements/base.txt are unused legacy artifacts (only referenced in old docs/superpowers planning notes). The inconsistency is a real hygiene/reproducibility wart that could bite a developer who manually installs from the stale files, but there is no automated version skew. Hence low, not medium.

title: torch version/CUDA pins inconsistent between compiled requirements.txt and requirements/{cpu,cuda}.txt
detail: The compiled requirements.txt pins torch==2.10.0 (line 575) together with CUDA 12.8 wheels (nvidia-*-cu12==12.8.*). But requirements/cuda.txt declares an unpinned `torch>=2.0.0` (line 6) and instructs installing from the CUDA 11.8 index (cu118, lines 2-4), and requirements/cpu.txt is likewise unpinned. These paths resolve to different torch versions and, worse, a different CUDA runtime (11.8 vs 12.8) than the locked environment. Per project memory the host runs CUDA 12/13, so the cu118 instructions are also stale.
failure_scenario: A developer follows requirements/cuda.txt and installs torch from the cu118 index on a CUDA 12/13 host, getting an older torch (latest cu118 build, not 2.10.0) with an 11.8 runtime, diverging from the requirements.txt/uv.lock-locked torch==2.10.0+cu128. Result: irreproducible torch/CUDA stack and potential runtime/ABI mismatches vs the locked env.
suggested_fix: Align the extra-index torch pins with the lock: pin torch (and the cu12x index) to match requirements.txt/uv.lock (torch==2.10.0, cu128), and update the cu118 comment. Better, generate these from a single lock rather than maintaining unpinned parallel files.
verify_reasoning: All factual claims verified by reading the files. requirements.txt is autogenerated by `uv pip compile pyproject.toml` and pins torch==2.10.0 (line 575) alongside CUDA 12.8 wheels (nvidia-*-cu12==12.8.*, lines 285-324). requirements/cuda.txt declares unpinned torch>=2.0.0 (line 6) and instructs installing from the cu118 index (lines 2-4); requirements/cpu.txt is likewise unpinned. So the version/CUDA divergence (torch 2.10.0/cu128 vs >=2.0.0/cu118) is real, and cu118 is indeed stale given the CUDA 12/13 host. The inconsistency is even broader than claimed: the actual backend Docker build (docker/backend/Dockerfile:25-27) uses pip install ".[api,cuda]" from pyproject (torch>=2.5.0) with the cu126 index — a third CUDA variant. Adversarial caveat: the requirements/ directory is orphaned — no build script, Dockerfile, or pyproject references it (grep outside docs returns nothing), and the setup_env.py its comments point to no longer exists. Thus the failure scenario requires a developer to manually follow a dead legacy file rather than the canonical pyproject/Docker path, so real-world impact is limited. The defect (stale, mutually contradictory pins/instructions) is genuine and correctly rated quality/low; if anything these files are dead code that should be deleted or regenerated.
